extracted.intended_audience: economists and education researchers estimating peer effects with survey data
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and empirical checks for estimating peer effects using class-level and student-level survey data (books at home measure), including tests for random assignment, regression/IV specifications, measurement-error corrections, and effect-size reporting. Focused on within- and across-school identification and robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pearson Chi² test for independence of characteristic and classroom assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Test statistic P = ∑∑ (ncj - n̂cj)^2 / n̂cj (under null of independence P ∼ χ² with (C–1)(J–1) degrees of freedom), where ncj is number of students with characteristic j in classroom c and n̂cj is predicted count under independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be aggregated across schools (summing S statistics) assuming schools are independent; test can only be carried out on the sub-sample of schools with two or more classrooms. Authors found in small Monte Carlo that the test generally performs well but rejects somewhat too often in samples of our size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting distribution of school-specific p-values for assignment randomness
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the null hypothesis of random assignment to classrooms, school-specific p-values should be (roughly) uniformly distributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Left-skewed distribution implies deliberate balancing (e.g., same fraction of girls in each class); right-skewed implies assignment of similar students to same classroom. Use histograms of p-values to detect non-random assignment for characteristics like immigrant status or language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of peer variable: leave-out classroom mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The peer variable for student i is the leave-out mean for the classroom, omitting student i's own value from the calculation of the mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used both for categorical fractions and for a 1–5 index; leave-out mean avoids mechanical correlation between individual's value and peer mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice between categorical peer fractions and index summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer/background variable can be represented nonparametrically as fractions of peers in several categories or summarized by an index (1–5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorical specification is most nonparametric but standard errors for categorical measures are often high, making inference difficult. The index provides a useful summary and is easier to interpret; in practice most variation occurs between specific categories (e.g., 26–100 vs 101–200 books).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression specification and controls (student, class, school, fixed effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with controls for student-level characteristics (gender, age, immigrant status, language at home, household size, individual books control). Then add class and school level covariates, school peer measures, and school fixed effects to test robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including class/school covariates often does little if they are uncorrelated with peer quality. Adding school-level peer measure or school fixed effects typically reduces estimated peer coefficient. Excluding schools that report ability grouping is a robustness check that often changes results little except in some countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-estimate across countries via inverse-variance weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: If peer effects are assumed the same across countries, combine country estimates by averaging the coefficients weighted by the inverse of the sampling variance to get a pooled estimate and its standard error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors compute weighted average of six country fixed-effects coefficients; standard error of meta-estimate is derived from sampling variances. Consider excluding countries with evidence of non-random assignment (Sweden) as sensitivity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement error consequences in peer regressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement error in the background variable affects both individual and peer regressors; classical measurement error attenuates coefficients, incomplete sampling of class increases attenuation, and school-level correlated shocks (ηcs) can introduce upward bias in OLS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of conflicting sources (attenuation from classical error vs upward bias from school-level correlation), net bias on OLS peer coefficient is ambiguous. Within-school (fixed effects) estimates correspond to ησ^2 = 0 and thus remove the upward bias but can exacerbate attenuation from measurement error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of instrumental variables to address measurement error
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrument parents' report of books at home with the child's report (and/or parents' education) for both individual and peer measures; IV converges to expression that solves classical measurement error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IV addresses classical measurement error (uσ^2 = 0 case) but does not resolve attenuation due to incomplete sampling of class. IV applied to within-school estimates plus sampling correction can recover larger peer effects. Also try IV with only student report as instrument as sensitivity check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusted IV estimator to correct sampling bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Within-school IV estimates can be adjusted for bias arising from sampling only a subset of students in a class using known class size (Ncs) and sample size in class (ncs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors propose an adjustment multiplier based on Ncs and ncs (adjustment in equation (13)) and report through Monte Carlo that this correction works well for their class-size variation. Use available Ncs and ncs in data to apply the adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument strength and diagnostics
rubrics_metrics.description: Check first-stage significance of instruments: t-statistics and F-statistics for relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors report t-statistics on instruments (students' report and parents' education) above 7 and F-statistics large, indicating little small-sample bias. Joint F-statistic > 10 used as rule-of-thumb (Netherlands exception where instruments not individually significant but joint F > 10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting standardized effect sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Report effect sizes as λ̂ * σ_X / σ_y, i.e., impact of a one standard deviation change in peer background in terms of student-level standard deviations of outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement error biases the observed σ_X; covariance between parents' and children's reports can be used to estimate variance of true variable under classical error assumption. Report country-level effect sizes and averages for comparability with literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include immigrant and foreign-language class fractions as robustness controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Include fraction of foreign-born children and fraction speaking a foreign language at home to probe whether non-random assignment of immigrants explains peer effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including these attenuates estimated peer effects at most slightly; re-estimate on sub-sample of schools with few immigrants as further robustness (but note sample size/power issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneity checks via interaction terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether peer effects vary across students by interacting the peer variable with an indicator of individual background (e.g., >100 books at home).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interaction coefficients to infer whether more heterogeneous classes benefit overall; authors find mixed patterns across countries and small, insignificant meta-estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monte Carlo experiments to validate tests and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Use small Monte Carlo experiments to assess performance of assignment tests and sampling/adjustment procedures under sample-size and class-size variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors used Monte Carlo to find Chi² test slightly over-rejects in sample size, and to validate that sampling-bias adjustment for IV works well for their observed class-size variation.
